opus-5.5.text:
I think the core difference comes down to what you actually have to simulate.

In autonomous driving, the car is mostly trying *not* to touch anything. The main job is perception and planning in a world that is, physically speaking, fairly simple: rigid vehicles, pedestrians, lanes, traffic lights. The dynamics of the car itself are well understood, and the interaction with the environment is mostly tire on road. So if your simulator renders the scene realistically and models other agents' behavior reasonably well, you get a lot of value. The hard part there is the long tail of scenarios, not the physics.

Embodied intelligence is the opposite. A robot is supposed to touch things. Grasping, pushing, folding, inserting, opening a drawer: every one of these is about contact. And contact is exactly where physics simulation is weakest. Friction, deformation, soft objects like cloth or food, cables, liquids, the tiny compliance in a gripper. Small errors in those models compound very quickly, so a policy that works perfectly in simulation can fail on the first try in the real world. That's the sim-to-real gap, and for manipulation it's much wider than for driving.

The second issue is diversity. Roads around the world look fairly similar structurally. Homes, kitchens, factories and warehouses don't. The number of object types, materials, articulations and layouts a robot might face is enormous, and building assets with accurate geometry *and* accurate physical properties for all of them is expensive. Visual realism you can increasingly get from generative models, but physical realism, meaning how heavy something is, how it bends, how slippery it is, is much harder to synthesize.

Third, there's the embodiment itself. In driving, the "body" is basically standardized: four wheels, steering, throttle, brake. In robotics, every arm, hand and humanoid has different kinematics, actuators, sensors and latencies. Data generated for one embodiment doesn't transfer cleanly to another, so you can't amortize your simulation effort the way the driving industry can.

And finally, driving had a data flywheel early on. Millions of cars on the road with cameras gave you huge amounts of real data, and simulation was a complement. Robotics doesn't have that fleet yet, so people hope simulation can be the *main* source, which puts far more pressure on its fidelity than driving ever did.

So my view is that simulation is very useful for things like locomotion, coarse motion, and pre-training visual understanding, but for fine-grained manipulation we still need a lot of real-world interaction data, and the realistic path is a mix: real data to anchor the physics, simulation and synthetic data to expand coverage.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts standardized cars with robots that have different kinematics, actuators, sensors, and latencies, and says data does not transfer cleanly across embodiments.

r002.rationale: It describes driving's main job as perception and planning in a physically simple world, and says realistic scene rendering provides substantial value.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core difference comes down to how much of the world you actually have to model.

In autonomous driving, the problem is surprisingly constrained. The car moves on a roughly two-dimensional plane. The road geometry is standardized, traffic rules are standardized, and the things you care about are mostly other vehicles, pedestrians, and lane markings. Most importantly, the car almost never touches anything. There's no contact physics. So if you build a simulator, you need good sensor rendering and reasonable agent behavior, but you don't need to get friction, deformation, or compliance right, because the vehicle isn't interacting with objects in that way. That's why simulation worked so well there, and why synthetic data could cover long-tail scenarios that would have been dangerous or impossible to collect on real roads.

Embodied intelligence, especially manipulation, is the opposite. The whole task is contact. A robot hand grasping a cup, folding a towel, inserting a plug into a socket. The success of each of those depends on tiny physical details: the friction coefficient of the surface, how a soft object deforms when you squeeze it, how a cable bends, how a liquid sloshes. Physics engines today are still quite poor at those things. Rigid body simulation is okay, but deformables, fluids, and especially articulated or soft materials are far from faithful. And when the physics is wrong, the policy learns the wrong thing, and it fails the moment it meets the real world. That's the sim-to-real gap, and in robotics it's much wider than in driving.

There's also a diversity problem. The driving world is one world: roads. The embodied world is every kitchen, every warehouse, every household, with millions of object categories and endless ways they can be arranged. You can't hand-model all of that. So people try generative approaches, world models, video generation, to synthesize scenes. But those models are good at visual plausibility and bad at physical consistency. A generated video might look right while an object passes through a table or a hand grabs something without actually closing. For a vision model that may be acceptable. For a robot that needs to act, it's not.

And finally, data in driving comes almost for free. Every car on the road with cameras is a data collector, and the human driver provides labels through their steering and braking. Robots don't have that. Real robot data has to be collected through teleoperation, which is slow and expensive, so there's enormous pressure to lean on simulation, exactly where simulation is weakest. That tension is, I think, the central bottleneck of the field right now. My own view is that simulation will matter, but more for pretraining, for learning rough priors and for stress-testing, while the last and hardest part will still have to come from real-world interaction data.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes variation in environments, objects, and contact physics, but does not attribute the difficulty to greater variation across robot embodiments.

r002.rationale: It mentions sensor rendering in driving simulation, but does not characterize autonomous driving as fundamentally a visual task.

astra-6.text:
I think the main difference is how much interaction you have to simulate. In autonomous driving, a lot of the problem is perceiving the environment and deciding how to move through it. Other road users react to you, of course, but in normal driving you’re trying to avoid physical contact. For an embodied robot, contact is often the whole point: grasping an object, opening a drawer, folding a piece of clothing.

That means visual realism alone isn’t enough. You also need the physics to be right. An object might look exactly right in simulation, but if its friction, weight, or stiffness is wrong, the robot can learn a strategy that fails in the real world. And those properties are often difficult to measure or infer from an image.

The other issue is diversity. Driving is enormously complex, but it has a relatively consistent structure: roads, lanes, vehicles, traffic rules. A robot working in a home encounters many different objects and tasks, and even two similar drawers can have very different mechanisms or resistance. Building simulations that capture that range is expensive.

So I’d separate generating more data from generating useful data. You can produce a huge number of synthetic interactions, but if they miss the physical details that determine success, the volume doesn’t solve the problem. Simulation is still valuable; the challenge is knowing which aspects need to be accurate and grounding them in real-world interaction.

r001.rationale: The response points to variation in household objects, tasks, and mechanisms, but does not attribute the difficulty to greater variation across embodiments than in autonomous driving.

r002.rationale: It says autonomous driving involves perceiving the environment and deciding how to move, but does not characterize it as fundamentally a visual task.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest difference is the range of interactions you need to simulate. In autonomous driving, the task is relatively well defined: the vehicle moves on roads, observes traffic, and makes driving decisions. It’s still very difficult, but much of the relevant information is about geometry, motion, and what other road users might do.

For embodied intelligence, especially manipulation, seeing the scene is only the beginning. When a robot picks up an object, success depends on friction, weight, stiffness, contact, and sometimes deformation. Two objects can look almost identical but behave very differently when you touch them. A simulation can produce a convincing image while getting those interactions wrong.

The diversity is also much greater. You have different objects, different environments, different robot bodies, and many possible tasks. That makes it difficult to know what your synthetic data needs to cover. And once the robot takes an action, any error in the simulated physics changes what happens next, so the mismatch can accumulate over a sequence of actions.

So I’d distinguish generating realistic observations from generating realistic experience. Simulation is very useful, but for embodied intelligence, the challenge is making the consequences of actions reliable enough that what the robot learns transfers to the real world.

r001.rationale: The response says embodied intelligence has much greater diversity, including different robot bodies, and links that diversity to the difficulty of covering synthetic data compared with the relatively well-defined driving task.

r002.rationale: It describes autonomous driving in terms of geometry, motion, and other road users, but does not characterize it as fundamentally a visual task.
